analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil and gas 'excess' profits and gives the money to low-income home energy assistance.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced with no cosponsors, referred to two House committees, and never brought to a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created an excise tax on profits from selling crude oil, natural gas, and fuels made from them. Profits above a level set by a new three-member 'Reasonable Profits Board' would be taxed at 50%, 75%, or 100% depending on how far they exceeded that level. All the money collected would go to the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), which helps low-income households pay heating and cooling bills. The bill was introduced in March 2009, sent to two House committees, and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households that receive LIHEAP help paying energy bills, since every dollar of the new tax would be added to the program's funding. The tax would also fall only on oil and gas profits above what a new board deemed 'reasonable,' so oil and gas companies would keep all profit up to that level and be taxed on the excess at rates starting at 50% and reaching 100%.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income households needing help with energy bills

how_it_helps.text: Dedicates the full proceeds of the windfall profit tax to the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, adding new federal money for low-income households' heating and cooling costs on top of normal appropriations.

Taxes only the portion of a sale's profit that exceeds a board-determined 'reasonable profit,' at graduated rates: 50% up to 2% over, 75% up to 5% over, and 100% beyond that, so ordinary profits are untouched.
Bars members and the director of the Reasonable Profits Board from having any financial interest in the businesses whose profits they judge, and pays them at government rates.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers and sellers, who would pay the tax on profits the new board judged excessive. Ordinary consumers could also be affected if sellers passed some of the tax into fuel prices, though the tax applies only to profits judged above a reasonable level.

drawbacks.text: The bill delegates the core judgment — what profit is 'reasonable' — to a three-member board appointed by the President, a standardless task that could produce arbitrary or politically influenced determinations and invited litigation.

An earlier federal windfall profits tax on crude oil, enacted in 1980 and repealed in 1988, is widely judged by economists to have reduced domestic oil production and raised federal administrative costs while collecting far less revenue than projected — a caution for any similar tax.

If sellers shifted some of the tax into prices at the pump or on heating bills, some of the cost would land on the same households LIHEAP is meant to help, and the bill contains no provision to prevent that.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea was straightforward: capture profits judged excessive during price spikes and redirect them to households least able to pay energy bills. The design was rough — 'reasonable profit' was undefined and left entirely to a presidentially appointed board, and the 1980s experience with a similar tax suggests such taxes can backfire on domestic production. Even so, the bill posed little risk to ordinary people and would have added dedicated funding to an existing energy-assistance program.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means and Appropriations committees from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote, and not a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Kanjorski introduced the bill on March 12, 2009.
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Appropriations Committee the same day; neither committee acted on it.
No member joined as a cosponsor.
No further action is recorded through the end of the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies were better off because the bill died: no windfall tax was ever imposed on their profits, and LIHEAP received none of the revenue it would have raised.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never acted on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a vote or even a cosponsor, so no partisan split is visible in the record; it was a single Democratic sponsor's bill that died without any recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill would have taxed 50% to 100% of profits judged above a 'reasonable' level on every sale of crude oil, natural gas, and their fuel products. Its death meant no tax was ever levied.

industries.industry: Oil and gas industry (windfall-profit-tax opponents generally)
industries.note: Windfall-profit-tax proposals draw industry-wide opposition on the argument that they penalize production and discourage investment; with the bill dead, the industry's tax treatment of these profits was unchanged.
